newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU opens probe into Lisnave rescue plan.
newsitem.headline: EU opens probe into Lisnave rescue plan.

text.p: The European Commission urged the Portuguese government of Thursday to inform it about recent measures to assist Lisnave, Europe's largest ship repairer company.

The Commission particularly queried the decision at the end of 1996 to grant guarantees to enable Lisnave-Estaleiros Navais de Lisboa to reschedule the reimbursement of a 6.0 billion escudo ($35.4 million) loan and to cover an overdraft facility of 3.5 billion escudos with a private bank.

In a notice published in the European Union's Official Journal, the Commission gave Portugal two months to back its case and to explain why a multibillion escudo restructuring plan approved by the EU in July 1995 failed.

Under the 1995 plan, Lisnave should have closed down its Margueira yard and transfer all ship repair work to Mitrena, south of Lisbon, by the end of last year. This was to result in a 35 percent reduction in capacity to 185 ships with an average tonnage of 70,000 tonnes a year, the notice said.

In return the Commission cleared total aid to the troubled ship repairer of 17.7 billion escudos and authorised the Portuguese state to pay 43 billion escudos in compensation for the closure of Margueira, effectively writing off Lisnave's debts.

"When the situation at 31 December 1996 is examined, there can be no doubt that the set of conditions which enabled the Commission to approve the restructuring aid are no longer met," the Commission said.

"The timetable has not been adhered to and the undertaking has not achieved the expected results, since it has had to rely on state guarantees in order to obtain the debt reschuduling and overdraft facility it needed in order to stay in business," it added.
The Commission must approve all measures intended to assist businesses in difficulty as they may contain state subsidies that can harm fair competition.

Earlier this month, it approved new measures to help restructure shipyards in Germany, Spain and Greece on the grounds that they had been hit by exceptional circumstances. All had benefited from state subsidies before.
Commission officials said at the time they were expecting Lisnave and unnamed French shipyards to submit fresh rescue plans.
Portuguese group Mello owns 48 percent of Lisnave, with the state holding 15 percent.
The firm's capital was written down tenfold earlier this month under an accord between the two main shareholders to save the company from collapsing.
